question: A 7-year-old child with pediculosis capitis has been treated correctly with permethrin 1% for two full cycles, but live lice persist at review. What is the most appropriate next step?

answers.text: Switch to malathion 0.5% lotion, continue wet-combing, and check close contacts for re-infestation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Persistent live lice after two correctly applied cycles of permethrin suggests permethrin resistance, which is well documented globally. The rational next step is a second-line pediculicide with a different mechanism — malathion 0.5% (an organophosphate) — combined with mechanical wet-combing and a check that close contacts have been treated, since re-infestation is equally common.

answers.text: Repeat permethrin 1% a third time at the same concentration

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Two correctly applied cycles have failed, making resistance — not incorrect application — the likely cause. A third attempt with the same agent and same mechanism of action is unlikely to succeed. Switching to an agent with a different mechanism (e.g. malathion) is the rational approach.

answers.text: Start a potent topical corticosteroid to control the scalp itch

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Topical corticosteroids have no pediculicidal action — the live lice will persist and reproduce. Treatment must target the parasite with an effective pediculicide, not just suppress the symptom of itch.

answers.text: Exclude the child from school until every nit has been removed

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Prolonged 'no-nit' school exclusion policies are no longer recommended — they cause unnecessary school absence and stigma without improving transmission control. The child can return to school after the first effective treatment. The priority is an effective pediculicide, not complete nit removal.

overallFeedback.feedback: When permethrin fails after correct use: switch the agent class (malathion 0.5%, an organophosphate), not the dose. Continue mechanical wet-combing. Check contacts for re-infestation. And remember — 'no-nit' policies are outdated; the child can attend school after effective treatment.

Permethrin resistance is common. When correctly applied permethrin fails, switch to malathion 0.5%, continue wet-combing as an adjunct, and always check that contacts have been treated — re-infestation from untreated contacts is as common a cause of persistence as true resistance.
